report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **supported, not false**—for **prescription, highly purified oral cannabidiol** used *in addition to* existing antiseizure medicines in children/adolescents with treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. It should not be generalized to over-the-counter CBD products.

A pivotal double-blind randomized trial (120 patients, 14 weeks) found median convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 per month with cannabidiol, versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo; the placebo-adjusted reduction was 22.8 percentage points (P=0.01). A later randomized dose-ranging trial independently found clinically meaningful reductions at both 10 and 20 mg/kg/day.

Reasons for caution, rather than rejection: trials were relatively short, studied a rare and severely affected population already receiving other drugs, and demonstrate an average reduction—not seizure freedom for everyone. Adverse effects were more frequent with cannabidiol, notably diarrhea, reduced appetite, sleepiness, and liver-enzyme elevations; monitoring and drug-interaction management (especially with clobazam and valproate) matter. The first trial was industry funded, but the result has been replicated and regulatory agencies approved pharmaceutical cannabidiol for this indication.

Thus, the defensible position is: **add-on pharmaceutical cannabidiol reduces convulsive seizure frequency on average, with meaningful harms and limitations—not that it has no effect.**
